title: New ID. AURA is the mainstream EV VW needs – but its software is the real story
content:
Volkswagen
Jo Borrás
| Nov 8 2026 - 5:42 am PT
Volkswagen built its global empire on the promise of affordable, accessible transportation, embodied by the iconic Type 1 Beetle.
Now facing an existential crisis after a decades-long push upmarket
, the automaker faces a reckoning – and a retreat back into affordable, mass-market electric sedans like the new FAW-VW ID. AURA L5 (and the software that powers it) might be
what VW needs to reach a new generation of buyers.
Like the Ford Model T, the original VW Type 1 Beetle was an engineering-led answer to a basic problem: making family transportation affordable and accessible to the masses. And regardless of how you feel about Elon Musk, the Tesla Model 3 has become the spiritual successor to those cars, bringing electric transportation to millions of mainstream drivers. As the Model 3 approaches its 11th year in public view, the recently revealed all-electric ID. AURA L5 and
VW JETTA
looks like it could be a compelling rival to the mainstream M3.
Co-developed by Volkswagen’s Chinese and German design teams and set to be built by the FAW-VW JV
, the ID. AURA L5 is an Accord/Camry-sized electric family car a practical fastback-style rear hatch, frameless doors, and a claimed “84.4% usable floor-area ratio.” The power-operated hatchback opens its maw more than 70 degrees, revealing a 39″ wide opening that can handle groceries, luggage, golf clubs, pets, bodies – whatever you got.
Don’t take my word for it, though. This is the original text from the company’s press release (translated from Chinese by Google):
The ID. AURA L5 is a pure electric family sedan, jointly designed by Chinese and German design teams, and highly replicates the design essence of the ID. AURA concept car shown at the 2025 Shanghai Auto Show. Its short overhang and long wheelbase proportions create a sleek and flowing coupe-like stance, achieving a “usable floor area ratio” of 84.4%. The sides feature true frameless doors, semi-concealed door handles, and an electric hatchback tailgate with an opening angle exceeding 70°, and an opening width exceeding 1000 mm, greatly improving the convenience of loading and unloading large items, deeply integrating fastback aesthetics with practicality. Some models will be equipped with LiDAR and feature the Hyper Sense 8 end-to-end large model, making daily travel easier and more convenient for customers.
VOLKSWAGEN GROUP CHINA
The production version of the ID. AURA L5 is expected to pack the same 155 kW (~208 hp) electric motors announced when the concept AURA L5 was first shown last year (battery specs were not released), and was shown as part of a broader product announcement of what VW Group China would be showcasing at this year’s China International Import Expo (CIIE). These include the first two models fully equipped with Volkswagen Group’s locally developed VEGA “integrated technology matrix” (read: software), and the Volkswagen Anhui intelligent pure electric “coupe” crossover.
Packed press release
FAW-VW ID. AURA L5.
The announcement coincides with reports from outlets like
that Volkswagen is evaluating whether to deploy its China-developed electrical architecture across the majority of its European markets.
“According to internal discussions confirmed by Group board member and Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer,” reports Autocar’s Greg Kable, “up to 75% of the firm’s core models in Europe could eventually use the China Electronic Architecture.”
The Volkswagen Group has been struggling to deliver a software experience that resonates with customers. To their credit, they’re looking for outside help,
spending billions of dollars on a software collaboration with EV startup Rivian
upcoming electric truck brand Scout
rather than going it alone. With billions of dollars and potential future of the company at stake, then, this seems like the most interesting bit of the announcement:
During the event, the immersive interactive experience exhibit “Digital Magic Cube,” which made its debut at last year’s China International Import Expo, will undergo an iterative upgrade to showcase the core strength of CEA (China Electronic Architecture), the software pillar of Volkswagen Group’s integrated self-developed technology matrix VEGA, to the attendees.
To date, CEA has enabled five new models from three joint ventures within the Volkswagen Group on a large scale, and software iterations have already been completed this year. CEA brings three core advantages to the Group’s new model lineup in China: intelligent accessibility, continuous upgrades, and safety redundancy. Through immersive interactive presentations, it provides consumers with the most intuitive experience. Empowered by the new AI R&D toolchain “C-Brain,” CEA introduces AI agents into software development, design, and engineering verification, enabling more flexible and efficient integration and innovation of vehicle intelligence capabilities, giving vehicles powerful thinking and perception abilities. Intelligent vehicles powered by CEA can better understand consumer needs, more efficiently create in-vehicle intelligent application scenarios, and better enhance digital intelligent safety redundancy, bringing Chinese consumers a new generation of intelligent mobility experience defined by Volkswagen standards
VOLKSWAGEN GROUP CHINA
The show runs through November 10th, and we’ll be keeping an eye out for more details on the ID. AURA lineup and the Anhui intelligent pure electric coupe, including its powertrain, battery, and software specifications, as they become available.

title: Everyone wants an electric pickup truck. I want more electric 125cc motorcycles
content:
Electric Motorcycles
electric trucks
Micah Toll
| Nov 8 2026 - 1:37 am PT
If you follow the EV industry in North America, you’d be forgiven for thinking that the future of transportation revolves around electric SUVs and pickups. Every week seems to bring another teaser from a startup promising to reinvent the family car or truck. The latest electric SUVs, “coming soon” tiny trucks, lifestyle trucks, modular trucks, etc. Companies like Slate, TELO, and countless others have generated plenty of excitement, even if many of them still have everything left to prove.
Don’t get me wrong – I hope they succeed. We need more affordable electric vehicles. But after spending nearly two decades covering a specific part of the electric-vehicle space and a good chunk of that time traveling around the world to see how people actually get around, I can’t help but wonder if we’re chasing the wrong prize here.
Because while the West keeps trying to electrify pickup trucks and SUVs, much of the world has already settled on a far more sensible transportation appliance.
It’s the
humble 125cc motorcycle.
The world’s default vehicle isn’t a car
Western readers often think of a sedan as the world’s “normal” or “sensible” vehicle.
But go traveling almost anywhere in Asia, and that illusion disappears in about five minutes.
The roads are filled with Honda Clicks and CG125s, Hero Splendors, Yamaha NMAXs and YBR125s, and countless other small-displacement motorcycles. They carry workers to jobs, students to school, families to dinner, and every imaginable cargo in between.
They’re the delivery vans. They’re the commuter cars. They’re grocery getters, family transportation, and work trucks. And perhaps more importantly, they transport hundreds of millions of people every single day.
You don’t have to spend long in places like the Philippines before realizing something else: these aren’t really “motorcycle cultures.” They’re just transportation cultures. People ride these machines because they make sense.
And I’ve
done it myself
to see what all the fuss was about. Sure, I’m an e-motorcycle guy through and through. But I’ve been there to ride a mile in their motorcycle sandals, and so I get it.
Even so, having had one cheek on each saddle, I still have to think there’s a better way than the tried-and-true 125cc combustion engine motorcycles that have become the workhorse of much of the world.
My time (briefly) testing a borrowed 125cc motorbike in the Philippines
Electric should be perfect here
The extreme proliferation of small motorcycles is what makes the current electric motorcycle market feel so strange. If there were ever a class of gasoline vehicle that batteries are already capable of replacing, it’s the 125cc combustion engine motorcycle.
These bikes aren’t demanding. They generally produce a modest 10-15 hp (8–11 kW) of power. They cruise comfortably around 45-60 mph (70-100 km/h). Most riders travel relatively short daily distances measured in dozens of miles, not hundreds.
A modern electric motorcycle with a 4-6 kWh battery can comfortably accomplish those same tasks while offering smoother acceleration, quieter operation, lower maintenance, and dramatically lower operating costs.
Unlike replacing a
heavy-duty pickup truck
that tows livestock trailers across Montana, replacing a 125cc commuter bike is already well within today’s battery technology. In many ways, it’s one of the easiest transportation sectors to electrify.
Royal Enfield’s Flying Flea C6 is one of the few examples of a light electric motorcycle designed for this role
Yet the West largely skipped this category
Instead, North America’s electric motorcycle market developed in an odd direction.
electric bicycles
, and those are great for urban commuters. But then we jump almost straight to
premium electric motorcycles
costing $15,000 to $25,000. The practical middle has remained surprisingly sparse.
Thankfully, that seems to be changing.
ONYX RCR
became something of a cult favorite by proving there was genuine demand for lightweight, motorcycle-like electric transportation without superbike performance.
Ryvid’s Anthem
pushed further, adding highway capability while still remaining approachable and relatively affordable.
LiveWire S4 Honcho
also feels like an encouraging step toward a lighter, more practical electric motorcycle instead of another oversized premium machine.
Infinite Machine’s Olto
, while occupying a slightly different category, demonstrates growing interest in practical urban electric two-wheelers that prioritize transportation over headline horsepower.
These companies are proving something important: People don’t necessarily need 100 horsepower. Many simply need transportation.
Infinite Machine’s Olto is a lightweight, easy-to-ride electric scooter that can carry two riders anywhere in a city
Maybe we’re obsessing over the wrong EV
Don’t misunderstand me. Electric pickup trucks absolutely have their place. Electric SUVs do too.
But we’ve spent the last decade pouring enormous engineering effort into electrifying some of the least energy-efficient passenger vehicles on the road.
Meanwhile, we’ve largely ignored one of the most efficient gasoline vehicle classes humanity has ever created.
A typical 125cc combustion engine motorcycle can already achieve fuel economy approaching or exceeding 100 mpg (2.35 liters/100 km). An electric equivalent becomes almost absurdly efficient.
We’re talking roughly 4-6 kWh per 100 kilometers (62 miles) – just a fraction of the energy consumed even by many compact electric cars. I once did the math, and a light electric motorcycle can travel 10,000 km (roughly 6,000 miles) for around $160 in electricity. Basically, your electrical bill doesn’t even notice when you own an electric motorcycle. Charging it simply doesn’t move the needle.
Instead of asking how we can fit ever-larger battery packs into increasingly larger SUVs and trucks, perhaps we should also be asking how many trips don’t need a large vehicle in the first place.
A Ryvid Anthem e-motorcycle could replace most car trips in the US, and the ‘fuel’ is so cheap that it’s almost free
Most trips don’t require two tons of metal
Transportation statistics across much of the developed world tell a familiar story.
Most trips involve one person. Maybe there’s also a backpack in the mix. Maybe there are some groceries getting picked up on the way home.
Occasionally
, there’s another passenger.
Those things are exactly what small motorcycles have been doing around the world for decades.
I recently spent some time in the Philippines, where I watched motorcycles carrying impossible-looking loads every day. Entire families would ride together. Construction materials. Furniture. Livestock. I saw two pigs on a 125cc bike, I kid you not. I’ve seen even crazier things in Thailand.
Again, I’m certainly not advocating that we adopt some of those practices in the West – there are obvious safety considerations – but it demonstrates just how incredibly capable these machines can be.
Even within normal Western expectations, a 125cc-class motorcycle is capable of handling an astonishing percentage of daily transportation needs.
My wife and I traveled everywhere we wanted to go in Menorca on a 110cc Honda
They don’t need to replace every car
This is where discussions about motorcycles often become unnecessarily polarized.
No, motorcycles aren’t ideal in every situation. Yes, heavy rain exists. Snow exists. Families with multiple children exist. Long interstate road trips exist.
Nobody is suggesting a 125cc electric motorcycle should replace every car.
But it doesn’t have to.
If a household can replace even half of its daily driving with a lightweight electric motorcycle, that’s already a massive reduction in energy consumption, congestion, parking demand, and transportation costs.
Transportation doesn’t have to be all-or-nothing. So enough with this “but what if it rains?” stuff. Either put on a jacket that day or drive your car. But for the majority of the trips each year you take where it’s not raining, you could have done it in a much more efficient (and fun) way.
Motorcycles work fine in the rain, and millions do it every day. The question is whether
work in the rain.
The infrastructure problem almost disappears
One of the biggest conversations surrounding EV adoption is charging. But smaller electric motorcycles barely participate in that problem. A 4-5 kWh battery charges overnight from an ordinary household outlet. The outlet you plug your laptop charger into is basically the equivalent of a Level 2 public charger for an e-motorcycle – that’s how fast it is.
DC fast charging isn’t really necessary on a light electric motorcycle. There’s no need for an expensive home charger. There’s no massive battery pack. Just plug it in before bed and wake up with a battery that’s been fully charged and waiting on you for hours already.
The simplicity is almost refreshing.
And if you want to go wild, there are swappable battery networks like
in Taiwan or
in South America that can make charging unnecessary.
Infinite Machine’s Olto battery even charges at home in a convenient little dock
They’re approachable
Another advantage rarely discussed is intimidation. Many people don’t want a 600 lb (270 kg) motorcycle producing superbike acceleration. They want something approachable, something lightweight, maneuverable, easy to park, and easy to live with.
That’s exactly why 125cc motorcycles became so successful globally.
Electric versions preserve all of those advantages while making them even easier to ride thanks to instant torque and the absence of clutch work. Many of them even come with reverse mode, making them easier to park and wiggle around even on hilly terrain.
LiveWire
S4 Honcho brings 125cc-equivalent electric motorcycles to the masses for an affordable $4,999 – and even has reverse!
Europe already understands the category
One reason Europe has seen more progress here is that the regulatory framework already exists.
Manufacturers regularly market bikes as “125cc equivalents,” and consumers immediately understand what that means.
Licensing systems and insurance companies recognize the category. It’s a mature transportation class.
North America, by comparison, often treats motorcycles as either recreational toys or large-displacement touring machines. We’ve largely forgotten that much of the world simply sees them as transportation.
The Yamaha XENTER E electric scooter brings 125cc-equivalent performance to Europe
A new generation is already telling us what it wants
Ironically, younger riders may already be showing us the way forward.
explosion in popularity
of Sur Ron-style electric motorcycles and lightweight e-motos demonstrates that younger generations are perfectly willing to embrace two-wheeled electric transportation.
Not everyone buying those bikes is looking for motocross. Many simply enjoy the freedom, accessibility, affordability, and fun that come with traveling on two wheels.
Rather than dismissing that trend, perhaps we should
recognize it as an opportunity
. Today’s recreational rider often becomes tomorrow’s commuter.
If someone discovers they enjoy getting around on an electric two-wheeler, moving from a lightweight e-moto to a practical 125cc-equivalent commuter becomes a much smaller leap than convincing someone to abandon their car entirely.
Teens today are riding small off-road electric dirt bikes, but those same riders could be tomorrow’s commuters
Maybe we’ve been looking in the wrong direction
One observation has stuck with me after so many years of covering the electric vehicle industry and traveling through countries where motorcycles dominate daily life. The West has spent years trying to electrify the largest, heaviest, and least efficient vehicles on our roads. Meanwhile, we’ve paid surprisingly little attention to electrifying the vehicle that already moves much of humanity every single day.
I’m not arguing that everyone should ride a motorcycle. And I’m certainly not arguing that cars no longer have an important place.
But perhaps we’ve underestimated just how many people could benefit from something in between.
Not just an electric bicycle, and not just a $25,000 electric motorcycle. Just an honest, practical, affordable electric equivalent of the vehicle that already keeps much of the world moving.
Because if we’re serious about accelerating electric transportation, maybe the future isn’t another electric pickup truck. Maybe it’s finally giving the world’s favorite motorcycle an electric motor.

title: Rolls-Royce gets a new Chinese rival as BYD unveils its Altior ultra-luxury electric limousine
content: Yangwang, BYD’s luxury brand, has unveiled the Altior (an ultra-luxury electric vehicle) in Abu Dhabi. Expected to be available for pre-order in China at around $311,540 (2,080,000 yuan), the new vehicle features rear-hinged coach doors, a four-seat cabin, and a range of bespoke interior and exterior features. Also known as the ‘Dingyao,’ the Altior is positioned to compete with other ultra-luxury vehicles like Rolls-Royce Ghost, Mercedes-Maybach S-Class, and Maextro S800. The Altior measures around 18.4 feet (5.6 meters) long and is effectively a four-seat executive limousine. But unlike competitors like Rolls-Royce, BYD’s new ultra-luxury car has one main competitive edge: its electric drivetrain and control systems. Its main selling points include four independent electric motors, one on each wheel. This should give the Altior precise traction and vehicle movement. BYD muscles in on Rolls-Royce’s territory It also reportedly comes with active suspension, meaning the vehicle uses cameras to detect approaching objects and other obstacles such as bumps. This allows the car’s suspension to anticipate rather than react to road conditions ahead. The Altior has a claimed range of 621 miles (1,000 km), though this is based on China’s Light-Duty Vehicle Test Cycle (CLTC) testing. A more realistic range under the Worldwide Harmonized Light Vehicle Test Procedure (WLTP) puts the range at something closer to 500 miles (805 km), though this has not been officially certified. The Altior reportedly supports charging from 10 percent to 70 percent in approximately five minutes using megawatt-capable chargers, although BYD has yet to confirm the vehicle’s full charging specifications. The Altior’s drivetrain reportedly allows tank turns, crab walking, and stability control following tire blowouts. Of its features, however, the four-motor system is arguably the most interesting and impressive. Conventional cars tend to rely on mechanical systems, brakes, and differentials to provide torque to each wheel. BYD’s system , however, can do this at the wheel directly and, in theory, independently. That allows capabilities such as rotating the vehicle almost on the spot and maintaining directional stability when a tire suddenly loses pressure. Such technology has potentially major implications beyond luxury vehicles, particularly for vehicle safety and off-road applications. These features are impressive, but could the Altior realistically challenge the likes of Rolls-Royce? Will the Altior succeed? Technologically, it certainly appears capable of competing. Commercially, however, that’s another question entirely. But Rolls-Royce ownership is more than just buying a piece of hardware; it is seen as a symbol of status and craftsmanship. It also has a long, storied heritage and reputation around the world. BYD doesn’t yet have the brand recognition in this area, which is not something you can just “speedrun.” It takes time. But the bigger picture is that Chinese automotive manufacturers like BYD are no longer satisfied with competing on price and production scale. They’re looking to move into the highest-margin, most prestigious segments of the global industry. And they’re attempting to do so with technology that traditional luxury manufacturers may struggle to match. Whether the gamble pays off remains to be seen, but it will be interesting to see how popular the Altior becomes.

title: North Korean ballistic missiles fired against US ally, power infrastructure targeted
content: A United States adversary’s missile system, KN-23, capable of evading the air defense systems, was behind the overnight strikes in Kyiv on November 7, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. ​Russia fired 36 short-range North Korean-made missiles to attack the key energy facilities in Ukraine, ahead of the winter months. Most of them were missed by the Ukrainian air defenses, which brought down only four of them, said Zelenskyy in a social media post. ​The North Korean KN-23 missile, known as Hwasong-11A in Pyongyang, is a ‘tactical guided weapon’ that can cover short ranges and be fired from a mobile launcher. The North Korean projectiles have design similarities with Russia’s Iskander-M missile and appear to have larger warheads and greater range. Escapes interceptor, greater range ​During the initial testing in May 2019, the missile had a range of 150-260 miles (240-420 kilometers), attaining a maximum height on the ballistic trajectory of 30-37 miles (50-60 km). The range improved further to nearly 270 miles (430 km) during another round of testing two months later. One of the missiles even flew about 430 miles (690 km), reaching a maximum height of 30 miles (50 km), according to missile defense advocacy. The results about the KN-23 top range were corroborated by experts from the U.S. Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS). ​The missile burns solid fuel and takes a low and flattened path for its flight, which shortens the flight time. This allows the ballistic missile to mask the enemy’s radar and interceptor systems because it does not follow a standard ballistic arc and has the capacity to maneuver during flight. ​In April this year, Ukraine’s defense ministry said that the KN-23 has been used in previous attacks on Ukraine, acknowledging that the weapon was “extremely difficult for air defense systems to deal with.” ​The enhanced navigation systems or an upgraded control mechanism that might enable better in-flight maneuverability might also improve its accuracy. ​Precision strike capacity However, the North Korean missile systems weren’t so precise to begin with. According to reports, Russia’s early firings of the KN-23, which began in early 2024, were often inaccurate. ​The launch and strike precision has been improved since December 2024, likely after the makers upgraded the design using data from the weapon’s combat use, it stated. ​According to Ukrainian officials, in December 2025, more than 20 ballistic missiles that were shot by Russia landed within 50 to 100 meters of intended targets, a  stark improvement from earlier strikes that often missed targets by 1000 to 3000 meters. ​The latest strikes hit substations in the Kyiv region that connect the Rivne and Khmelnytskyi nuclear power plants to Kyiv and central Ukraine. Other substations in the Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Rivne, Kharkiv, and Dnipropetrovsk regions were also damaged, as Russia also launched 172 drones in the attack . ​On October 30, the U.S. State Department approved a potential sale of 500 Patriot air defense interceptor missiles, the main Ukrainian defense against ballistic missiles, to Ukraine by a major American defense supplier, Lockheed Martin. ​

title: Scientists uncover cannabis from 2,800-year-old Siberian tomb, may have ritual ties
content: Scientists detected chemical traces consistent with cannabis’ psychoactive compounds in preserved human hair recovered from an ancient Siberian tomb. An international team led by Gino Caspari of the University of Bern and the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology analyzed remains from the Tunnug 1 princely tomb in Russia’s Tyva Republic. The burial belonged to high-ranking members of the Scythians, a horse-riding culture that roamed the Eurasian steppe. The findings provide what the researchers described as the oldest directly dated archaeological evidence that cannabis was used for its intoxicating properties about 2,800 years ago. Cannabis may have ritual links Researchers recovered about 1,000 cannabis seeds from the burial chamber that they could confirm were deposited in the early eighth century B.C.E. The seeds show that cannabis played a role in the rituals surrounding the burial. However, researchers couldn’t confirm how they integrated it into the ritual. Furthermore, researchers emphasized that cannabis seeds alone couldn’t establish whether the plant was consumed for its intoxicating effects. That being said, cannabis has historically served several purposes, including serving as material for oil and fiber. However, plant materials such as flowers, leaves, and resins rarely survive the test of time, so they often do not appear in archaeological contexts. To investigate further, researchers analyzed preserved human hair recovered from the central burial chamber. With high-resolution mass spectrometry, they identified clear signals consistent with cannabinol (CBN) in several hair samples. Through the oxidation of tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), CBN, the primary intoxicating compound in cannabis, can form. Additionally, researchers detected weaker signals that were consistent with THC, based on their mass, according to the University of Bern. “This study is particularly insightful because it combines the analysis of plant remains with molecular traces in the human body,” said Caspari. Hair samples laced with weed The findings suggest that at least some members of the ancient Siberian elite consumed weed for its intoxicating effects. “The molecular traces in the hair and the cannabis seeds… suggest that cannabis was used for its intoxicating properties,” Caspari said. However, the researchers could not determine how much cannabis was consumed or whether it was inhaled or ingested. The evidence also suggests cannabis played a role in Scythian funerary rituals. The plant remains were recovered alongside elaborate burial offerings, including at least 18 horses arranged around the burial mound, several dozen additional horse sacrifices, and scattered human bones that researchers said indicate human sacrifice. The team believes the cannabis seeds most likely came from wild plants, although it remains unclear whether they had been cultivated or selectively bred to contain higher concentrations of psychoactive compounds. The study highlighted that some wild cannabis populations across Eurasia may naturally have contained elevated levels of these compounds. Researchers are continuing to investigate the plant remains through genetic analysis. “We have already begun sequencing some of the plant samples,” said Caspari. “DNA preservation is excellent in this case. This will help us learn more about the history of the domestication and spread of this crop soon,” he added. The findings were published recently in Science .

title: 251% faster: Heavy rain could speed up Alaskan glacier surging nearly 25 feet a day
content: Heavy rainfall can increase the speed of an Alaskan glacier by as much as 251 percent during its slow-flow phase, according to a new study examining how precipitation influences glacier movement during both surge and quiescent periods. Boise State University researchers analyzed GPS measurements from Turner Glacier (Sít’ Kusá) in Alaska. They compared rainfall-driven speed changes during a surge between 2020 and 2021 with a slower-flow period from 2022 to 2024. The findings showed that rainfall can accelerate the glacier in both phases, although the frequency, magnitude, and duration of these speed-up events differ depending on the glacier’s state. Rainfall alters glacier speed Surge-type glaciers undergo periodic order-of-magnitude increases in flow speed, reaching rates higher than their usual movement, the study found. To investigate these effects, researchers compared 10 GPS-derived glacier surface speed records with modeled rainfall estimates. According to the study, GPS instruments installed around the glacier recorded its position every 15 seconds. Researchers also compared rainfall estimates with measurements from a weather station at nearby Yakutat Airport. The researchers identified speed anomalies by comparing short-term and long-term average speeds. They examined the duration, magnitude, and timing of these changes following large rainfall events. During the 2020–2021 surge, nine of 16 large rainfall events, or 56 percent, recorded speed anomalies. The glacier reached speeds of 24.6 feet per day, representing a 116 percent increase. These acceleration events lasted an average of 66.5 hours, the study found. Between 2022 and 2024, rainfall-induced accelera ti on occurred less frequently. Of 37 rainfall events, 17 showed speed-ups, or 46 percent. These events produced smaller speed changes of approximately 1.5 meters (4.9 feet) per day and lasted around 33 hours. However, the percentage increase was considerably greater, reaching 251 percent. According to the team, acceleration during the surge generally began about 12 hours after rainfall started, while speed increases during quiescence peaked approximately 32 hours after rainfall began. The study reported that acceleration was greatest in the glacier’s lower sections during both phases, compared with areas higher in the valley. Drainage changes during surge The researchers examined these speed changes to understand better how the glacier’s drainage system responds to rainfall. Glacier drainage efficiency influences how water moves beneath the ice. According to the team, inefficient drainage can allow water pressure to build beneath a glacier, reducing friction between the ice and the ground. The study found that differences in acceleration characteristics indicated more efficient drainage during quiescence. However, rainfall-induced acceleration occurred during both phases, suggesting that an inefficient component of the drainage system persisted throughout the glacier’s surge cycle. The researchers also found that particularly large and prolonged rainfall events could temporarily slow the glacier during its surge. Speeds subsequently returned to pre-event levels in less than two weeks as the drainage system reverted to its inefficient state. The findings support recent research that suggests glacier drainage systems do not simply switch between two configurations during surge cycles. According to study authors, the results demonstrate that rainfall can affect the movement of both fast- and slow-flowing glaciers, helping scientists to understand how glacier speeds respond to precipitation.

title: NASA Space Telescope Meets Fiery End After Nearly 22 Years in Orbit
content:
Built to last just two years, NASA’s Swift Observatory finally fell back to Earth after nearly 22 years of uncovering the universe’s most explosive secrets. Credit: NASA
NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has returned to Earth after spending nearly 22 years in space, bringing an extraordinary mission of cosmic discovery to an end. The spacecraft reentered Earth’s atmosphere on Wednesday, more than two decades after launching in 2004.
Swift was a pioneering space observatory equipped with three telescopes capable of detecting different wavelengths of light. It was the first observatory of its kind, built to investigate some of the most powerful explosions in the universe.
NASA’s Swift Observatory Reenters Earth’s Atmosphere
The U.S. Space Force confirmed that Swift entered the atmosphere at 7:39 a.m. EST on November 4, above North Sumatra, Indonesia. The reported location was approximately 3.4 degrees north latitude and 98.6 degrees east longitude.
NASA anticipated that most of the spacecraft would burn up as it plunged through the atmosphere, although some pieces may have survived the descent.
A Two-Year Mission That Lasted Nearly 22 Years
When Swift launched in 2004, its primary goal was to study gamma-ray bursts, extraordinarily energetic explosions that rank among the most powerful events in the cosmos. The observatory was initially expected to operate for just two years, but it continued collecting valuable scientific data for more than two decades.
Over its remarkable lifetime, Swift became an exceptionally versatile tool for astronomers. Its instruments could observe several types of light, allowing researchers to investigate a wide range of cosmic phenomena. The spacecraft could also quickly turn toward sudden, short-lived bursts of energy and notify other observatories, giving scientists an opportunity to study events that might otherwise disappear before they could be examined.
These capabilities helped transform our understanding of the universe. Swift contributed to discoveries involving active galaxies powered by supermassive black holes, stars producing powerful X-ray flares, and the spectacular explosions of dying stars known as supernovas. Its observations also extended much closer to home, providing valuable information about comets and asteroids traveling through our own solar system.
What began as a two-year mission ultimately became nearly 22 years of exploring the universe, leaving behind a remarkable scientific legacy.

title: NASA’s Perseverance Mars Rover Just Drove Farther Than Any Vehicle Beyond Earth
content:
NASA’s Perseverance Mars rover took a selfie with several of the 10 sample tubes it deposited at a sample depot it is creating within an area of Jezero Crater nicknamed “Three Forks.” Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS
NASA’s self-driving Perseverance rover has broken the all-time off-world driving record and is now exploring ancient Martian terrain that could hold clues to the Red Planet’s long-lost history.
NASA’s Perseverance rover has set a new record for driving on another world, traveling farther across the surface of Mars than any vehicle in history. On October 11, its total distance reached 28.10 miles (45.22 kilometers), surpassing the previous record of 28.06 miles (45.16 kilometers) held by NASA’s Opportunity rover, which operated on Mars from 2004 to 2018. Perseverance achieved the milestone on its 2,006th Martian day, known as a sol, completing in just five and a half years a journey that took Opportunity nearly 15.
The record was broken as Perseverance
made its way toward
a location called “Idubi,” passing through an area nicknamed “Lac de Charmes” just beyond the western edge of Jezero Crater. Scientists believe this region contains some of the most ancient terrain ever investigated in the solar system. Comparable rocks on Earth have largely disappeared because of erosion and plate tectonics (Mars doesn’t have tectonic plates). At Idubi, researchers hope to uncover evidence of ancient hydrothermal systems, where hot water once interacted with surrounding rock.
How NASA’s Self-Driving Mars Rover Broke the Record
A major reason Perseverance has been able to travel so far is its sophisticated autonomous driving technology. Its navigation system, called AutoNav, allows the rover to analyze its surroundings and choose a safe route while moving. As it drives, Perseverance captures images, creates three-dimensional maps of potential obstacles, and determines how to travel between destinations chosen by engineers on Earth. NASA describes this ability as “thinking while driving.”
Unlike earlier rovers, Perseverance can perform these calculations while traveling at or close to its maximum speed. It has covered as much as 1,351 feet (412 meters) in a single Martian day. More than 90% of its total driving distance has involved AutoNav evaluating the terrain, a dramatic improvement over the roughly 5% achieved by the first Martian AutoNav system used by
Opportunity
and its twin rover, Spirit.
The difference in computing capability is equally remarkable. NASA’s first Mars rover, Sojourner, relied on just 20 measurement points to evaluate the ground ahead. Perseverance now analyzes 600,000 points every time it examines the terrain.
One of Perseverance’s navigation cameras captured this shot on October 11, 2026, the Martian day, or sol, that a 299.6-foot (91.31-meter) drive pushed the rover’s total mileage past Opportunity’s 28.06-mile (45.16-kilometer) record on Mars. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech
“It is an honor to be working on Perseverance at a moment when the technology has evolved to the point that drives like these are routine,” said Steven Lee, the project manager of the
Curiosity
and Perseverance rovers at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. “The original mission called for no more than 12.4 miles of driving. We’ve blown well past that, and with all mobility systems fully operational and favorable extended-ground-life test results, we expect Perseverance to keep adding to this record for many years to come.”
NASA has already authorized the first extension of the Perseverance mission. The extended phase began in October and is expected to keep the rover investigating the rim of Jezero Crater through approximately the end of 2028.
Nearly 30 Years of Mars Rover Exploration
Perseverance’s accomplishment builds on nearly three decades of robotic exploration on Mars. With each new generation, NASA has developed rovers capable of traveling greater distances and navigating increasingly challenging landscapes.
The journey began in 1997 with Sojourner, a small rover roughly the size of a microwave oven. During its 83-sol mission, it traveled approximately 330 feet (100 meters). In 2004, NASA sent the much larger, golf-cart-sized rovers Spirit and Opportunity to Mars. Although both were originally designed for missions lasting just 90 sols, they went on to far exceed expectations.
Spirit traveled 4.8 miles (7.7 kilometers) before its mission ended during the harsh Martian winter of 2010. Opportunity proved even more durable, operating for 5,111 sols and completing the first marathon-distance drive on another world in 2015. Its extraordinary journey established the distance record that Perseverance has now broken.
Curiosity rover
, which arrived at Gale Crater in 2012 and continues exploring Mars, has accumulated more than 23.65 miles (38.07 kilometers) of driving.
This infographic illustrates the distances driven by various rovers on the surface of Earth’s Moon and Mars. Of the vehicles shown, the NASA Mars rovers Perseverance and Curiosity are still operational and moving across the surface; the figures shown for those two are distances driven as of October 11, 2026. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech
A Smarter Mars Rover That Keeps Improving
Perseverance is not simply traveling farther than its predecessors. Its ability to navigate independently has continued to improve since it landed on Mars.
“The rover that broke this record did so by making its own decisions about the path. Given the autonomy to just go, Perseverance is a better driver than the one that landed, and we’re not done,” Mark Maimone, deputy team chief for robotic operations on Perseverance. “Our newest software teaches Perseverance to steer less and roll more, and to check its own position against orbital maps mid-drive. The next frontier is sunlight itself. Glare in the navigation cameras is why we park by mid-afternoon if we’re driving toward the Sun, and if we can teach the rover to see past those artifacts, every rover that follows gets a longer working day.”
Before surpassing Opportunity’s Mars record, Perseverance had already traveled farther than vehicles driven on the Moon. Its journey exceeded the 22.2 miles (35.7 kilometers) covered by Apollo 17 astronauts Gene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt in 1972, as well as the 24.2 miles (39 kilometers) traveled by the Soviet Lunokhod 2 rover in 1973.
These achievements demonstrate how much robotic mobility has advanced, but setting records is not the mission’s primary objective. The real advantage of traveling farther and faster is that scientists can investigate more locations, examine a wider variety of rocks, and piece together a more complete picture of Mars’ ancient history.
Searching for Ancient Life in 4-Billion-Year-Old Rocks
Perseverance’s growing range has allowed it to explore several dramatically different Martian environments. Its journey began on the floor of an ancient lake, continued through the remains of a long-vanished river system, and eventually brought it to the rim of Jezero Crater.
Along the way, the rover discovered a rock called “Cheyava Falls” containing a potential
biosignature
, a feature that could provide evidence of ancient biological activity. Scientists are now investigating another type of environment that may once have offered conditions suitable for life: hydrothermal systems associated with heated water and rock.
So far, Perseverance has gathered
29 samples of rock and regolith
, the loose material covering the Martian surface. These samples represent several distinct geological settings, including the crater floor, a delta formed by an ancient river, and the surrounding crater rim.
Near the rim, the rover has been studying rocks formed or altered by powerful impacts roughly 4 billion years ago. These formations preserve evidence from an extremely early period of planetary history, much of which has been destroyed or transformed by geological processes on Earth.
After completing its investigation of Lac de Charmes, Perseverance is expected to continue following the crater rim before turning south during its extended mission. One of its destinations is Rainbow Falls, an enormous block of ancient crust measuring 328 feet (100 meters) across that was pushed upward by the impact responsible for creating Jezero Crater.
With its driving systems still functioning and years of additional exploration planned, Perseverance is positioned to keep extending its record while uncovering new clues about the Red Planet’s distant past.

title: Look Up: Three Meteor Showers, a Supermoon, and a Historic Space First Are Coming in November
content:
Three meteor showers, dazzling fireballs, a brilliant supermoon, and Voyager 1’s historic journey one light-day from Earth make November a remarkable month for skywatchers. Credit: Shutterstock
November offers plenty of reasons to look up, including the Taurid and Leonid meteor showers, a close pairing of Mars and Jupiter, a remarkable milestone for NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft, and a bright supermoon.
November Skywatching Highlights
Around November 5:
The Southern Taurid meteor shower reaches its peak, with the possibility of unusually bright fireballs.
Around November 12:
The Northern Taurids peak, producing roughly five meteors per hour under ideal viewing conditions.
November 15 and 16:
Mars and Jupiter appear just 1.2 degrees apart in the sky before sunrise.
November 17:
NASA celebrates Voyager 1’s historic journey with its Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day activation.
November 17 and 18:
The Leonid meteor shower offers up to approximately 15 meteors per hour under ideal conditions, with the best viewing before dawn after the Moon sets.
November 24:
A full supermoon brightens the evening sky, beginning a sequence of three consecutive supermoons.
Taurid Meteor Showers Could Produce Brilliant Fireballs
November begins with two opportunities to catch meteors streaking through the darkness. The Southern Taurids reach their peak around November 5, followed by the Northern Taurids approximately one week later, around November 12.
Both showers take their names from the constellation Taurus. Although the meteors travel across different parts of the sky, they appear to originate from two distinct regions within this constellation.
Neither shower is particularly active compared with some of the year’s bigger meteor displays. Under ideal conditions, each typically produces about five meteors per hour. However, the Taurids are known for occasionally generating exceptionally bright meteors called fireballs, which can make even a relatively quiet night of skywatching memorable.
A full Moon rises over Vasquez Rocks Natural Area and Nature Center north of Los Angeles, California, on June 24, 2021. Credit: NASA/Preston Dyches
Leonid Meteor Shower Peaks November 17 and 18
The next major meteor display arrives later in the month, when the Leonids become the focus of attention.
For the best chance of seeing them, head outside during the early morning hours of November 17 or 18, once the Moon has dropped below the horizon. With favorable conditions, observers could see as many as 15 meteors per hour, although actual counts will generally be lower.
A few simple preparations can make a significant difference. Choose a viewing location away from bright city lights, allow approximately 30 minutes for your eyes to adjust to the darkness, and find a comfortable position that gives you a broad view of the sky.
A sky chart showing where to look for the Leonids in November 2026. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech
Mars and Jupiter Appear Side by Side Before Sunrise
Meteor showers are not the only attraction this November. Two of the solar system’s most recognizable planets will also put on an impressive display.
Before sunrise on November 15 and 16, look toward the southeastern sky to find Mars and Jupiter appearing remarkably close together.
The planets will be separated by approximately 1.2 degrees, slightly more than the combined apparent width of two full Moons. Jupiter will stand out as the brighter object, while Mars will be visible nearby with its distinctive reddish color.
No telescope or binoculars are required to enjoy the pairing, since both planets can be seen with the naked eye. Although they remain separated by enormous distances in space, their positions relative to Earth make them appear close together in our sky.
Observers who check their positions over several consecutive mornings can watch the two planets gradually approach one another before appearing to move apart again.
A sky chart showing Mars and Jupiter close in the night sky. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech
Voyager 1 Reaches a Historic One Light-Day Milestone
Far beyond the planets visible in November’s morning sky, NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft is approaching an unprecedented achievement.
During November, Voyager 1 will become the first human-made object to reach a distance of one light-day from Earth. This means the spacecraft will be so far away that even a signal traveling at the speed of light will need 24 hours to reach it.
Receiving a response will require another 24 hours, bringing the total communication time for a signal and its reply to approximately two full days.
Artist’s rendering of a NASA Voyager spacecraft traveling through interstellar space. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech
The spacecraft is much too distant to be seen, but skywatchers can get a sense of its direction by locating Ophiuchus, the constellation also known as the Serpent Bearer. Voyager 1 is traveling in that general direction as it continues its journey into interstellar space.
To recognize this historic achievement, NASA is inviting the public to participate in its Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day activation on November 17.
A night sky chart highlights the location of Voyager 1 within the constellation Ophiuchus on November 17 around 5 p.m., looking toward the western horizon. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech
November’s Supermoon Begins a Three-Month Series
The month concludes with another eye-catching event when a full supermoon rises on November 24.
The Moon does not travel around Earth in a perfectly circular orbit. Instead, its slightly elliptical path causes its distance from our planet to vary throughout the month.
When a full Moon occurs while the Moon is relatively close to Earth, it is commonly called a supermoon. From our perspective, it appears somewhat larger and brighter than an average full Moon, although the visual difference is often difficult to notice.
November’s supermoon is particularly notable because it marks the beginning of three consecutive months featuring supermoons, with additional events arriving in December and January.
For a memorable view, look toward the eastern horizon around sunset as the full Moon begins to rise. It may seem enormous when positioned close to the horizon, but this apparent increase in size is largely caused by a familiar visual phenomenon called the Moon illusion.
The effect can occur with any full Moon, regardless of its actual distance from Earth, making November’s moonrise an especially appealing opportunity to experience it.
Here are the phases of the Moon for November:
Moon phases for November 2026, showing the dates for Third Quarter, New Moon, First Quarter, Full “Supermoon,” and a concluding Third Quarter in Pacific Time. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech

title: Scientists Finally Crack a 1,600-Year-Old Roman Glass Mystery
content:
Chemistry
A modern glass sculpture inspired by the ancient Roman Lycurgus Cup demonstrates the remarkable properties of dichroic glass, appearing green in reflected light and glowing red-orange when light passes through it. Credit: Ed Cartledge, Sort of Films
More than 1,600 years after the Romans created the famous Lycurgus Cup, a University of Sheffield technician has found a way to reliably reproduce its extraordinary color-changing glass.
A glass cup made more than 1,600 years ago has puzzled historians and glassmakers for centuries.
When light reflects off its surface, the cup appears jade green. When light shines through it, the glass turns a striking ruby red. Despite knowing much about the science behind this unusual effect, modern glassmakers have struggled to reproduce it consistently. Now, researchers at the University of Sheffield have developed a recipe that recreates the remarkable color-changing properties of this ancient Roman masterpiece.
Lycurgus Cup
, created in the fourth century AD and housed in the British Museum, is made from a special type of glass known as dichroic glass. Its appearance changes depending on whether light reflects from the surface or passes through the material. The cup is one of only 40 surviving Roman glass cage cups and among the most complete. It is also the only surviving example known to display this extraordinary color-changing effect.
Its craftsmanship is just as remarkable as its colors. The decoration depicts Lycurgus, a mythical Thracian king, entangled in vines as punishment for his misdeeds. In 2022, an international panel of artists and conservators recognized the cup as one of the seven glass wonders of the world, honoring its artistry, unusual colors, and exceptional preservation.
Gold and silver behind the color shift
Scientists believe the secret lies in tiny amounts of gold and silver added to the glass by Roman craftspeople. Under the right conditions, these metals can form layered nanoparticles thousands of times smaller than a grain of sand. Because the particles are smaller than the wavelengths of visible light, they absorb light strongly and produce vibrant colors that depend on their size and shape.
Dr. Lisa Hollands, a University of Sheffield glass expert. Credit: Ed Cartledge, Sort of Films
Understanding this process, however, is different from knowing exactly how to recreate it. The precise techniques used by Roman glassmakers remain unknown, and previous attempts to reproduce the effect have met with varying degrees of success.
Modern experiments recreate Roman colors
The challenge took on new life when Christina Metcalfe, project manager for the Molecular Photonic Breadboards project, asked University of Sheffield technician Dr. Lisa Hollands to recreate the glass for the university’s LightFest in 2025.
“I knew that making a glass of this type was likely to be a complex task, as it is not just a case of adding nanoparticles to glass,” said Dr. Hollands, from the University’s School of Chemical, Materials and Biological Engineering.
“I’ve studied and worked with glass for over 25 years, so I used the knowledge and experience I’ve gained, coupled with a modern scientific understanding of what I was trying to achieve.
“To start with, I worked with a leading Roman glass expert, Professor Caroline Jackson, to research what was already known about glass of the time and developed a base glass using modern materials to mimic what the Romans might have used. Then came the more difficult part of trying to get small amounts of gold and silver into the glass in the right form.
“Although if the Romans could have seen me experimenting, they’d probably laugh and ask: ‘Why does she not know how to make this?’”
Glass artist Elliot Walker works with specially developed dichroic glass. Credit: Ed Cartledge, Sort of Films
Hollands experimented with different types of furnaces, starting materials, and oxygen levels, even testing the addition of sugar. After numerous attempts, she developed a glass that appeared opaque green under reflected light but turned red when illuminated from behind. The successful sample demonstrated that the distinctive optical effect of the ancient cup could be recreated using modern materials and experimental techniques, although it did not establish the exact recipe used by the Romans.
The first piece was exhibited at LightFest, an event held in Sheffield by the Molecular Photonic Breadboards project in partnership with the Universities of Sheffield and Bristol. Funded by the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (EPSRC), the project focuses on developing materials that harness light for sustainable technologies. These materials could support fields important to the United Kingdom’s economy, including solar energy, quantum technologies, and healthcare diagnostics.
Roman glass inspires a modern sculpture
With the glass recipe established, the team wanted to create something that would showcase its unusual properties while paying tribute to the original Roman artifact.
“The next step was to commission a piece worthy of paying homage to its illustrious predecessor.
“We approached Elliot Walker, one of the UK’s finest glass artists and winner of season two of Netflix’s Blown Away, who accepted the challenge and was commissioned to create a contemporary sculpture using Dr Hollands’ recipe,” said Metcalfe.
For Walker, working with a material inspired by ancient glassmaking offered a rare connection to the craftspeople who had mastered similar techniques centuries earlier.
“It is a very rare thing to have the opportunity to work with glass developed from ancient mixtures and recipes, and it is always a very exciting one.
“You can really get an idea of how the glass makers of the past would have adapted to this sort of glass; it’s like shaking their hands.”
Walker drew inspiration from both the story depicted on the Lycurgus Cup and the classical Farnese Atlas sculpture. His design also needed to make the unusual optical effect visible to viewers, which influenced the final form of the artwork.
“I wanted to keep the sculpture quite classical in form and to carry through the original story of Lycurgus shown on the cup, but we needed a blown element within this to really show the dichroic glass,” Walker explained.
“The piece is a blend of the Lycurgus story and the Farnese Atlas sculpture, with the globe replaced by a cup.”
The completed sculpture is scheduled to be unveiled at the Millennium Gallery during the University of Sheffield’s
Festival of the Mind
, running from November 6 to 15, 2026. After the festival, it will become a permanent exhibit at the
Turner Museum of Glass
, located within the university’s School of Chemical, Materials and Biological Engineering.
“We set out to create something tangible to help the public understand what is possible when these tiny nanoparticles are embedded in something,” Metcalfe said.
“What Lisa and Elliot have managed to achieve has surpassed all our expectations. The incredible historic narrative really captures people’s imaginations, and I like to think we’ve created something that people will marvel at for years to come.”
Glassmaking insights for nuclear waste storage
Although this particular glass is expected to have mainly decorative uses, the knowledge gained from recreating it could contribute to the development of new photonic materials and advanced glasses for managing radioactive waste.
The project also connects with ongoing research led by Professor Russell Hand at the university’s Immobilisation Science Laboratory (ISL), within the School of Chemical, Materials and Biological Engineering. His work focuses on immobilizing complex nuclear wastes in glass, a process intended to keep hazardous materials safely contained.

title: Scientists Discover Something Unexpected 90 Kilometers Beneath Earth
content:
A rock’s extraordinary 90-kilometer journey beneath Earth has exposed a hidden heat mystery that challenges scientists’ understanding of the planet’s interior. Credit: Stock
A rock from Papua New Guinea was hotter than expected during its descent into Earth, challenging models of a process that influences earthquakes, volcanoes, and climate.
Earth recycles its own surface. In regions called subduction zones, one tectonic plate, a vast slab of Earth’s outer shell, sinks beneath another as the plates collide. These zones are sites of earthquakes and volcanic activity, and they help stabilize Earth’s climate over millions of years by recycling molecules such as carbon dioxide.
A rock from Papua New Guinea has revealed a gap in scientists’ understanding of the temperatures inside these regions. Four million years ago, it descended more than 90 kilometers, or about 56 miles, below Earth’s surface. But roughly halfway down, it was already much hotter than current models would predict.
Taleba Bay vista , Goodenough Island in the Milne Bay province of Papua New Guinea. The sample investigated in this study was collected from an outcrop in Taleba Bay. Credit: Paul Fitzgerald
Minerals record a descent beyond 56 miles
An international research team led by Göttingen University reconstructed the journey by studying eclogite, a red and green rock that forms under the high pressures found in subduction zones. Minerals within the rock preserve evidence of the conditions it experienced underground, allowing researchers to piece together its history. The findings were published in
Nature Geoscience
Using a combination of analytical techniques, the researchers found tiny inclusions of coesite trapped inside another mineral during the rock’s formation. Coesite is a mineral that requires extremely high pressure to form. Its presence helped the team conclude that the rock had reached a depth of at least 90 kilometers, where it experienced temperatures of around 800°C, or 1,470 °F.
The larger image (left) is a close-up of one of the red garnet crystals on the eclogite. The microscope has zoomed in to this crystal to show a tiny coesite inclusion which proves a subduction depth of more than 90 km. The inclusion is a bit smaller than 1 µm – approximately one hundredth the size of the thickness of a human hair. Credit: Reproduced from Schönig, J., Ferrero, S., Gresky, K. et al. Geothermal gradient change during subduction recorded by ultrahigh-pressure eclogite. Nature Geoscience (2026). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41561-026-02110-1
Unexpected shallow heat challenges subduction models
At about 45 kilometers, or 28 miles, however, the rock had been only 100°C cooler, a difference of 180°F. In other words, it had already reached around 700°C, or 1,290°F, at roughly half the depth. Those shallower conditions were unusually hot, while the deeper conditions fit the more common, relatively cold pattern of subduction. Calling the deeper conditions cold does not mean the rock cooled as it sank. It means that its temperature was lower relative to its depth than it had been earlier in the journey.
Dr. Jan Schönig at Göttingen University’s Geoscience Center explains, “Finding this change from hot to cold subduction was unexpected, as this contradicts our current thermal models of subduction zones.”
Researchers have found rocks that recorded unexpectedly high temperatures before. This is the first time, though, that a rock’s journey from shallow to deep conditions has so clearly shown an accompanying shift to relatively colder temperatures for its depth.
Microscope image of a thin section from the eclogite – the rock which was studied for this research. It formed at ultrahigh-pressure and the image shows its distinctive red-and-green crystals which gave information about its unusual journey. Credit: J Schönig/Göttingen University
Two explanations for the excess heat
One possible explanation is that shearing stress, produced as plates move against one another, heats rocks at shallow depths more than scientists have assumed. Another is that the subduction zone had not yet had enough time to develop the lower temperatures expected there. Both processes could have contributed.
Understanding these temperatures more accurately could help researchers assess how subduction affects earthquakes, volcanic activity, and the movement of chemicals through Earth, including the long-term carbon cycle. It could also clarify how subduction has operated over millions to billions of years and how it continues today.
Dr. Jan Schönig. Credit: Dr. Jan Schönig
Reference: “Geothermal gradient change during subduction recorded by ultrahigh-pressure eclogite” by Jan Schönig, Silvio Ferrero, Kerstin Gresky, Dominik Sorger, Axel K. Schmitt, Bernd Wunder, Suzanne L. Baldwin and Adam F. Holt, 1 October 2026,
Nature Geoscience
DOI: 10.1038/s41561-026-02110-1

title: Popular Dairy Alternatives Could Be Leaving You Short of Essential Nutrients
content:
Plant-based dairy alternatives, including oat, almond, soy, and coconut milk products, are increasingly popular substitutes for traditional dairy. Although they offer options for people following vegan or dairy-free diets, their nutritional content varies, and many lack essential nutrients such as iodine, calcium, and vitamin B12 unless fortified. Credit: Shutterstock
A new study reveals that even partially replacing dairy products with plant-based alternatives could significantly reduce the intake of essential nutrients.
Replacing even a modest amount of dairy with plant-based alternatives could significantly reduce essential nutrient intake, according to a new study from the University of Surrey. Researchers found that substituting just 20% to 35% of dairy products increased the estimated prevalence of inadequate iodine intake among adolescent girls from 54% to 65%. Among women ages 19 to 49, the figure rose from 32% to 42%.
The study also identified reductions in calcium, riboflavin, and vitamin B12 intake. However, researchers found that fortifying plant-based alternatives and other foods could help prevent these nutritional shortfalls.
How Plant-Based Alternatives Affect Nutrient Intake
In the first UK study of its kind, researchers from the University of Surrey and Queen’s University Belfast analyzed dietary data from more than 3,500 people, ages 18 months to 100 years. Using the National Diet and Nutrition Survey, they modeled how replacing milk, yogurt, and cheese with commercially available plant-based alternatives would affect intake of four essential micronutrients.
Dr Katie Nicol, a research fellow at the University of Surrey and co-author of the study, explained:
“With the growing need to address environmental sustainability, many dietary recommendations are focused on plant-based diets and the reduced intake of animal products.”
“With the rise in plant-based alternative foods, we need to know whether they are like-for-like replacements for the micronutrients that are found in dairy products. This is particularly important for vulnerable groups, including young children and adolescent females, who are more likely to be deficient in certain micronutrients, which could affect their overall health.”
Why Iodine Deficiency Is a Major Concern
Iodine was the nutrient most affected by dairy replacement. When researchers modeled completely replacing dairy with plant-based alternatives under current fortification levels, the estimated prevalence of inadequate iodine intake reached 80% among adolescent girls and 72% among adolescent boys. These figures reflect modeled dietary inadequacy, not confirmed clinical deficiencies.
Iodine is essential for producing thyroid hormones, which regulate metabolism and support growth and brain development. It is particularly important before and during pregnancy, when iodine requirements increase.
Dr Sarah Bath, associate professor at the University of Surrey and lead author, said:
“The UK is particularly vulnerable to iodine insufficiency due to a lack of an iodine fortification policy such as universal salt iodization, which many other countries have.”
“People may also be unaware of the importance of iodine, which is needed to make thyroid hormones to regulate our metabolism, support healthy growth, and brain development. Iodine is particularly important during pregnancy, when the requirement increases, but it is also essential prior to pregnancy to ensure that stores are optimized. People are also unaware that dairy products are a major source of iodine, particularly in the UK, and that plant-based alternatives, unless fortified, have a very low iodine content.”
Fortified Foods Could Reduce Nutritional Risks
The researchers found that mandatory fortification of plant-based dairy alternatives could prevent declines in micronutrient intake. However, even with fortified alternatives, an estimated 59% of adolescent girls would still have inadequate iodine intake. Adding iodine to bread reduced that figure to 37%, suggesting that combining both fortification strategies could be more effective.
Dr Nicol emphasized the importance of aligning nutrition policies with environmental goals:
“Nutrition policy must evolve in tandem with environmental targets; however, it is important that shifts towards more sustainable diets do not compromise on public health. Fortification of foods is one way that this could be achieved; however, government policy is needed to make this happen.”
How Researchers Tested Dairy Replacement
Dr Anne Nugent, from Queen’s University Belfast, described how the team identified dairy-containing foods in the UK National Diet and Nutrition Survey and modeled replacing them with equal amounts of plant-based alternatives. The researchers accounted for differences in the nutritional content of available products and tested whether fortification could prevent deficiencies without causing excessive nutrient intake.
“During the analysis, we first identified all foods and recipes containing dairy produce (milk, cheese, and yogurt) in the national food survey for the UK, the National Diet and Nutrition Survey. Next, we conducted a series of replacement scenarios whereby we substituted the dairy present with an equal weight of plant-based dairy alternatives. As the nutrient composition of dairy alternatives available on our supermarket shelves can vary, we also applied a condition to make sure that every dairy alternative we had identified in our previous market survey had an equal chance of selection. The last step was to examine the impact on dietary intakes of key nutrients following either the reduction or removal of dairy from the diet, replacing it with the dairy alternatives as above, and asking whether a series of fortification options could mitigate against any shortfalls in intake while avoid situations of excess.”
Reference: “The impact of replacing dairy products with plant-based dairy alternatives on iodine and other micronutrients: a modelling study and evaluation of policy options to support population intake” by Katie Nicol, Anne P Nugent, Jayne V Woodside, Kathryn H Hart and Sarah C Bath, ,
The Lancet Planetary Health
DOI: 10.1016/j.lanplh.2026.101515

title: A Healthier Form of Salt Could Prevent Nearly 3 Million Deaths Every Year, Scientists Say
content:
Excessive salt consumption can raise blood pressure, increasing the risk of heart disease, stroke, and kidney damage. High sodium intake can also contribute to fluid retention and place additional strain on the heart and blood vessels. Credit: Stock
A global study spanning 193 countries suggests that a simple change to everyday salt could prevent millions of deaths and cases of cardiovascular and kidney disease each year.
Replacing ordinary salt with a potassium-enriched alternative could prevent nearly three million deaths worldwide each year, according to a new study covering 193 countries. Researchers estimate that a global switch could also prevent more than ten million new cases of cardiovascular and kidney disease annually, offering a potentially powerful way to reduce the health burden of high blood pressure.
The analysis, led by The George Institute for Global Health, examined how different levels of salt replacement might affect the world’s 4.6 billion adults. The findings suggest that even limited changes, particularly among people already diagnosed with high blood pressure, could produce substantial health gains.
How a Simple Salt Substitute Could Protect Health
Potassium-enriched salt replaces part of the sodium chloride in regular table salt with potassium chloride. It looks, tastes, and performs much like conventional salt in cooking but contains less sodium and provides additional potassium, two changes that can help lower blood pressure.
“Consuming too much sodium and not enough potassium are well established causes of high blood pressure, a major risk factor for life-threatening conditions like strokes, heart attacks and kidney disease. Switching to potassium-enriched salt addresses both these dietary issues at the same time, with substantial health benefits,” said Bruce Neal, Senior Professorial Fellow at The George Institute.
High blood pressure (hypertension) affects approximately 1.4 billion adults aged 30 to 79 worldwide, or roughly one in three people in that age group. Cardiovascular disease (CVD) caused 19.2 million deaths in 2023, nearly 50 percent more than three decades earlier. In 2025, the World Health Organization (WHO) endorsed potassium-enriched salt as a way to reduce blood pressure and cardiovascular risk.
Major Health Benefits Without a Complete Switch
The researchers modeled several scenarios, including replacing all salt consumed at home, in restaurants, and in processed foods. Switching only household table salt could prevent approximately 1.85 million deaths and 6.19 million new cases of cardiovascular and chronic kidney disease annually. Replacing salt exclusively in processed and restaurant foods could prevent another estimated 1.56 million deaths and 5.46 million new disease cases each year under that separate scenario.
More targeted approaches also showed considerable potential. If 80 percent of people with diagnosed hypertension switched their household salt, the model projected approximately 590,000 fewer deaths annually. Among those receiving treatment for hypertension, a comparable level of adoption could prevent about 480,000 deaths each year.
“While a global shift from regular salt to a potassium-enriched substitute is aspirational, this is a starting point to get countries thinking about the opportunity, with much greater potential and at much lower cost than many drug-based treatments,” Neal said.
Which Countries Could Benefit Most?
The projected benefits varied considerably between countries. Under a complete replacement scenario, China could prevent approximately 1.08 million deaths and 3.61 million new cardiovascular and kidney disease cases annually. India could avert nearly 400,000 deaths and 1.53 million new cases, while the United States could prevent approximately 105,000 deaths and 492,000 new cases.
Achieving these reductions would require strategies tailored to how people consume salt. In many countries, household cooking accounts for a substantial share of sodium intake. In Europe and North America, however, processed and restaurant foods contribute more than 70 percent, making cooperation from food manufacturers and restaurants essential.
“To realize the maximum benefits from switching to potassium-enriched salt, we need to see the food industry in Europe and North America, where over 70% of salt intake comes from processed and restaurant foods, get on board. This would also require investigating ways to scale up the production of potassium chloride to meet demand,” Neal said.
What About the Risks of Extra Potassium?
Although potassium-enriched salt can help lower blood pressure, it may pose risks for people whose kidneys cannot effectively remove excess potassium from the bloodstream. This can lead to hyperkalemia, a potentially dangerous condition that can disrupt the heart’s electrical activity. People with advanced kidney disease and those taking certain medications that increase blood potassium levels require particular caution.
The study’s modeling suggested that the overall health benefits could outweigh the risks even among people with advanced kidney disease. However, that population-level finding does not mean potassium-enriched salt is safe for every individual.
“People with serious kidney disease and those taking medications that significantly raise blood potassium levels need to take precautions. Risks for this group can be managed effectively through patient education, product labeling, and clinical oversight,” said Professor Vivek Jha, a nephrologist and Senior Professorial Fellow at The George Institute in India.
Reference: “Global health outcomes from replacing dietary sodium chloride with potassium-enriched salt” by Liping Huang, Xiaoyue Xu, Kunihiro Matsushita, Tammy M. Brady, Lawrence J. Appel, Ewout J. Hoorn, Aletta E. Schutte, Jason H. Y. Wu, Maoyi Tian, Leopold N. Aminde, Kathy Trieu, Bruce Neal and Matti Marklund, 4 November 2026,
Nature Health
DOI: 10.1038/s44360-026-00216-9

title: Scientists Engineer Rice That Fights Back Against a Devastating Crop Disease
content:
Scientists have developed a new way to protect rice from a destructive bacterial disease that threatens harvests worldwide. Credit: Shutterstock
An AI-designed gene-editing tool is opening new possibilities for protecting essential food crops.
An artificial intelligence-designed gene-editing tool has helped scientists develop rice plants resistant to bacterial blight, a destructive disease that threatens harvests across Asia and Africa. Researchers at the University of Missouri achieved the result using a technology previously tested in animal cells, opening a potential new route to protecting one of the world’s most important food crops.
The breakthrough centers on OpenCRISPR-1, a gene-editing system developed by California biotechnology company Profluent. Led by Bing Yang, a Curators’ Distinguished Professor in the College of Agriculture, Food and Natural Resources, the Missouri team adapted the technology for use in rice.
An AI-Designed Tool for Stronger Crops
Gene editing allows scientists to make targeted changes to DNA, including modifications to genes that influence a plant’s vulnerability to disease. By studying how bacterial pathogens interact with rice at the genetic level, researchers can identify opportunities to strengthen the crop’s defenses.
OpenCRISPR-1 also offers an advantage over some existing gene-editing systems: it is freely available for research and commercial crop development.
Bing Yang. Credit: University of Missouri
“Unlike proprietary gene-editing tools that may require licensing agreements for commercial use, OpenCRISPR-1 is open source and free for research and commercialization of crop genome editing,” Yang said. “That accessibility gives researchers and companies greater flexibility to explore new genetic solutions and develop crop varieties with valuable agricultural traits.”
Protecting Rice From a Devastating Disease
Bacterial blight can severely reduce both the quantity and quality of rice harvests. In regions where rice farming supports millions of livelihoods, outbreaks can have serious economic consequences and threaten a vital food supply.
“Bacterial blight can wreak havoc on rice crops, reducing both yield and quality, which creates serious challenges for farmers who depend on the staple grain,” Yang said. “Our lab investigates how bacterial blight interacts with rice at the genetic level — knowledge that helps us identify ways to strengthen the plant’s natural defenses.”
Although the researchers have successfully developed resistant plants, the work remains at the laboratory stage. The next challenge is transferring the findings into commercially grown rice varieties, followed by additional testing, regulatory review, and partnerships with companies capable of bringing the crops to market.
Could the Technology Protect Other Crops?
Farmers may have to wait several years before rice varieties developed through this research become available. Meanwhile, Yang’s team sees potential applications beyond bacterial blight, including improving resistance to other diseases and helping crops withstand environmental stresses.
Corn and soybeans are among the crops that could eventually benefit from similar genetic approaches, although such applications would require further research.
“Our recent breakthrough paves the way to explore genetic solutions to a range of challenges that farmers face across Missouri and nationwide, from devastating plant diseases to drought and extreme temperatures,” Yang, an investigator in the Bond Life Sciences Center, said. “By developing crops that are better equipped to withstand these stresses, we can help farmers protect yields, strengthen agricultural resilience and prepare for an increasingly challenging growing environment.”
Reference: “AI-designed OpenCRISPR-1 enables efficient targeted mutagenesis and prime editing in rice” by Ajay Gupta, Rabia Ahuja, Bo Liu, Mark Adero, Dung Thi Pham, Wolf B. Frommer and Bing Yang, 20 May 2026,
aBIOTECH
DOI: 10.1016/j.abiote.2026.100054
